arms_compared.why: minilm_vector is the strongest arm that needs no graph structure, so it is what the structural signal has to beat to have earned its cost

budget_and_timeouts.reading: every cutoff falls on a fresh logic or mathematics query, three per query, always the last three of the shortlist. Those graphs are larger than the coding ones and exact edit distance on them exhausts the two-second budget after seven comparisons. The arm is already at its declared ceiling on a corpus of eighty pairs.

conclusion: The named structural error class is real but small: seven of twenty-six residual queries. Nineteen are shortlist-ceiling misses that no reranker can reach. The usefulness floor Gate D1 missed is therefore a candidate-generation shortfall, not a structural-comparison shortfall, and the cheapest lever against it needs no new code.

projected_maximum_gain.method: a reranker can only reorder what the shortlist admits, so the perfect ordering of the current ten-candidate shortlist bounds every reranker, including any future one. Diagnostic, not a benchmark arm.

replay.checked: minilm_vector 0.5375 / 0.4392 and the graph arm 0.6750 / 0.4481 with 60 budget cutoffs, identical to sprint-21d1-retrieval-benchmark.json
replay.database_access: none; the report replays from committed artifacts alone
replay.source_pairs: the 80 pair artifacts named by sprint-21d1-emg-root.json, read from the D1 evidence artifact store and checked against their persisted pair hashes
replay.source_queries: sprint-21d1-graph-queries.json; every rebuilt query's content hash was compared with the frozen manifest before it was used

no_relevant_candidate_in_pool.meaning: group exclusion removed every relevant pair. None occurred.

rerank_ordering.meaning: a relevant pair was on the shortlist and the graph score failed to lift it into the top five. This is the only class a better structural comparator could address.

shortlist_ceiling.meaning: no relevant pair reached the vector shortlist, so the reranker never saw one. Unreachable by any reranker, this one or a future one.

regressions.reading: three queries the vector arm answered and the graph rerank lost. In all three the relevant pair sits in the arm's *highest* score block and still lands at rank seven, because that block holds more than five candidates and their order is the pair-id tiebreak. The two truth-table queries are the sharpest case: the vector arm ranked the relevant pair first and the graph rerank pushed it to seventh without ever scoring it below anything.

score_degeneracy.reading: bounded graph edit distance carries about one bit per query here. Each query yields exactly two distinct scores and the whole corpus yields six. For the twenty fresh logic and mathematics queries every comparison that completed returned the same 0.525424, so within that stratum the arm expresses no preference at all and the order is the pair-id tiebreak. The arm's advantage is a coarse binary split, not a ranking.
score_degeneracy.why_it_still_beats_the_vector_arm: the binary split is informative even at one bit: it puts a shortlisted relevant pair into the top five for 54 of the 61 queries that had one, where an arbitrary reordering of the same shortlist would place about half.

shortlist_is_the_binding_constraint.method: rank the whole eligible pool with the vector arm and record where the first relevant pair lands. Diagnostic, not a benchmark arm, and no number here is a reported D1 metric.
shortlist_is_the_binding_constraint.reading: every relevant pair is already within the vector arm's top thirty of a seventy-eight candidate pool. Widening the shortlist from ten to twenty lifts the ceiling for any reranker from 0.7625 to 0.9750 and costs no dependency at all. The reranker is not what caps this system; the shortlist width is.
